title: Anthropic pitches AI safety bill that may block a model if 50+ people could be killed
content:
Over the past year, concerns have swirled over the potential dangers posed by artificial intelligence, and debates have raged over the proper path for AI safety. Now, Anthropic appears to have put forth its own vision for how the government might regulate its industry.
Politico recently reported that the AI lab has been shopping around a new draft bill on AI safety that it hopes Congress might consider adopting. The legislation posits certain scenarios in which the release of an AI model could be blocked from distribution.
Those scenarios involve a “foreseeable, imminent risk” — one in which over 50 people are at risk of dying or if over a billion dollars in property damage could result, Politico writes. The catastrophic risk in question must “stem from the creation or release of a biological weapon, the model evading its developer’s controls or a cyberattack,” the outlet notes.
The metrics offered here — 50 people and a billion dollars — are similar to those in a piece of California legislation that was recently passed into law, Senate Bill 53, which similarly defined those scenarios as tantamount to “catastrophic risk.”
Anthropic’s bill suggests that analysis of a model’s potential for disaster could be arrived at via the use of “independent evaluators” who would be registered with the U.S. Commerce Department. These evaluators could potentially be paid by the AI labs themselves — so long as the “payment is not contingent on the evaluations’ results,” Politico writes.
It’s not clear how this proposed system would ensure that payments couldn’t influence the evaluation. Demis Hassabis, chairman of DeepMind, posited some months ago that a self-governing AI regulatory body should mimic the financial industry’s Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA).
In Anthropic’s draft bill, when evaluators determine that an imminent catastrophic risk is posed, they would have 72 hours to contact the Commerce Department about it. The Commerce Department would then have to request to a Washington, D.C., judge a halt to the model’s release. The legislation would expressly forbid any federal agency from having the discretion to halt the model’s distribution on its own, Politico writes.
Anthropic did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment, but a spokesperson did confirm the draft bill to Politico. “This bill represents the proposals outlined in Anthropic’s Advanced AI Framework, which we have been advocating for with federal and state lawmakers since June,” the spokesperson said.
The theoretical risks offered in the draft policy are a little bit far afield from the kinds of incidents that have been top of mind for the tech industry of late. While there are people warning of the potential of human death, the primary concern has largely been the threat of agentic hacking. A rash of incidents in which AI programs have apparently disobeyed their human operators and hacked websites on the open internet has spurred concern that models may be lacking proper security controls.
In an effort to present a solution to the spectacle of crisis that the labs themselves have helped bring about, companies like Anthropic have offered up their own preferred solutions.
Indeed, despite labs’ perpetual warnings that the technology they’re selling could result in the demise of human civilization, they have largely been resistant to mandatory government oversight. Instead, they have suggested a voluntary system of embedded evaluators — supposedly “neutral” third-party observers who are placed inside AI organizations to monitor the models for potential signs of risk or abuse.
Still, Anthropic’s mere suggestion for legislation appears to go slightly further than others’ regulatory proposals offered by the industry, including Nvidia, whose CEO, Jensen Huang, recently argued that the AI industry didn’t need any new laws at all.

report.summary: Anthropic推AI安全法案，拟设模型发布阻断门槛
report.background: 过去一年，AI安全争论升温：实验室一边警告灾难性风险，一边抵制强制监管，倾向自愿嵌入评估员。加州SB 53已用“50人死亡或10亿美元损失”定义灾难风险，Anthropic草案被视为将该思路推向联邦；同时，近期AI代理越权黑客事件让网络安全风险更受关注。
key_points: 草案设“可预见、迫近风险”门槛：50人死亡或10亿美元财产损失，且须源于生物武器、模型逃逸控制或网络攻击。
评估由商务部注册的独立评估员进行，可由AI实验室付费但不得与结果挂钩，外界仍质疑利益冲突。
流程是评估员72小时内报告商务部，商务部向华盛顿特区法官申请暂停发布，联邦机构不能自行叫停。
阈值与加州SB 53相似，Anthropic称源自其6月Advanced AI Framework，显示州法思路正向联邦复制。
行业监管分歧明显：Anthropic主张立法，英伟达黄仁勋称不需要新法；实验室普遍偏好自愿评估而非强制监管。
report.impact: 对AI行业，若草案成法，前沿模型发布前将多一道司法审查和第三方评估，合规成本与延迟上升，评估市场兴起。开发者需准备红队、风险评测和审计记录，尤其生物、网络与失控场景。普通用户可能遇到高风险模型延迟发布或下架，安全透明度提升，但创新节奏可能受抑。
report.tools: 想跟进可关注：英国AISI的Inspect评估框架、METR任务标准、Garak与PyRIT红队工具、MLCommons AILuminate基准；可用于模型风险评测、越狱及网络/生物滥用场景测试。
